title: The bird that leads humans to honey
text:
Somewhere in the grasslands and forests of Africa lives a small, plain-looking bird with an extraordinary talent. The greater honeyguide does not sing the most beautiful song, and it does not have the brightest feathers. Its fame comes from a remarkable partnership with people.

A sweet reward

Honeyguides love beeswax and the grubs of bees, but a bees' nest is hard to reach. It is guarded by thousands of angry insects, and it is often hidden high in a tree or deep in a rock. The bird cannot break the nest open itself. People, however, can. With smoke and tools, they open the nest and take the honey. The bird feeds on what is left behind.

How the partnership works

When a honeyguide finds a nest, it flies towards honey hunters and calls loudly. Then it flits from tree to tree, always in the direction of the nest, waiting for the people to catch up. Hunters in countries such as Mozambique and Tanzania have their own special whistles and calls to answer the bird. Studies have shown that a honeyguide is far more likely to lead a person who uses the traditional call than one who makes some other sound.

Could this be only a coincidence? In a study published in 2016, researchers tested the idea in northern Mozambique. They played three types of sounds to see how often the birds appeared. Honeyguides were about twice as likely to lead the hunters when the traditional call was used as when the other sounds were played. This suggests that the birds really do understand the call.

Why it matters

Experts believe this is one of the few examples of wild animals and humans cooperating to hunt. It also shows that animals can learn from the sounds that humans make, and that the partnership may have developed over thousands of years. Sadly, as people turn to sugar from shops instead of wild honey, fewer hunters call to the birds, and the tradition is fading.

Perhaps the lesson is that nature has been talking to us all along. We simply need to know how to listen.
